title: The two smallest growth rates of coefficient patterns of powers of binary polynomials are 3 and 1+√5 (Garbe's Conjecture 3.7)
source: Kevin Garbe, “Patterns In The Coefficients Of Powers Of Polynomials Over A Finite Field”, arXiv:1304.4635 (2013), Conjecture 3.7. https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.4635

significance.root_decision: The conjecture holds for every polynomial over the field with two elements that has at least two nonzero terms: the growth rate λ of the number of nonzero coefficients in the first 2^k powers of f is at least 3, it equals 3 exactly when f is similar to 1+x, there is no value strictly between 3 and 1+√5, and it equals 1+√5 exactly when f is similar to 1+x+x^2. The bound λ ≥ 3 is short: after removing common powers every state of the section recursion has at least three children. The gap and the two classifications need more: multiplicities are projected modulo the direction of f, each three-way choice is deferred for a fixed number of steps, and states are weighted by (1+√5) to the number of pending choices; a count to any fixed depth cannot give 1+√5, as the polynomials 1+x+x^(2^m) show. For monomials the rate is 2 and for the zero polynomial it is 1, so the first sentence of the conjecture as printed fails there; the source's own tables and remarks concern non-monomials only. Lean defines the cumulative count, the growth rate as the limit of its k-th root along 2^k, and similarity as the equivalence relation generated by shift, dilation, reversal and powers, and proves the full statement for polynomials with at least two terms, as well as the values 2 and 1 in the degenerate cases.
significance.caveat: Counted in corrected form: the statement is proved for every binary polynomial with at least two nonzero terms; as printed, the first sentence fails for monomials (rate 2) and for the zero polynomial (rate 1), which Lean also proves; the source's introduction, Table 4 and the remark after Theorem 3.9 show that monomials were not intended. One link is outside Lean: the source defines λ as the Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue of a matrix and states that it is the growth rate of the cumulative counts; Lean formalizes the growth rate. The source's justification (irreducibility of the matrix) is false for most rules, but the identification holds for every f by a spectral-radius argument given in the paper and checked numerically by the final check on all 1,023 rules of degree at most 10 and all 30 values of the source's Table 4. 'Similar' is the equivalence relation generated by the transformations of the source's Theorem 3.6 (the one-way reading would make the conjecture false at (1+x)^2). The bound λ ≥ 3 and the case λ = 3 are short; the content is the gap and the classification at 1+√5. The source is a high-school research paper with little exposure (three citing works on another topic). The papers of Willson, of von Haeseler, Peitgen and Skordev, and of Takahashi were not read in full (reviewer's probability that one settles the conjecture: about 0.03). All work is by AI and no human has checked it: the proof, the Lean code and the paper are by GPT-6.2 Sol lanes; the adversarial review before Lean (not routine 0.72) and the final check (0.70) are by two separate Claude Opus 5.5 lanes.
